title: Money for Nothing
description: The only American No. 1 for the most video-skeptical band of the MTV era — a borrowed appliance-store rant turned into a blockbuster, wrapped in the decade's most famous blocky computer cartoon.

pops.text: The narrator isn't Mark Knopfler. He was shopping in a New York appliance store when he overheard a deliveryman in a baseball cap ranting at a wall of MTV-tuned TVs — so he borrowed pen and paper and wrote the guy's actual words down on the spot.

Sting just happened to be vacationing on Montserrat during the AIR Studios sessions, dropped by, and improvised the falsetto 'I want my MTV' hook — a phrase lifted straight from the network's own advertising slogan. Because its melody echoed The Police's 'Don't Stand So Close to Me,' Sting landed an official co-writing credit.

Knopfler's riff was a deliberate chase of ZZ Top's Eliminator-era crunch — he even asked Billy Gibbons how he got the sound. Gibbons guarded his secrets and later joked Knopfler did a half-decent job considering he'd told him nothing.

The riff's famous nasal bite was pure luck: a Shure SM57 slipped off its stand overnight at Montserrat, and the resulting phase cancellation became the record's sound. The team tried to recreate it later in New York and never could.

The blocky movers were built by Ian Pearson and Gavin Blair at London's Rushes Postproduction on a Bosch FGS-4000 system. The pair later founded Mainframe, the studio behind ReBoot — the first-ever CGI TV series — plus Beast Wars and most of the Barbie movies.
The video was directed by Steve Barron, the man behind 'Billie Jean' and A-Ha's 'Take On Me' — and it beat 'Take On Me' for Video of the Year at the 1986 MTV Video Music Awards.

Across 11 total VMA nominations, the video won Video of the Year and Best Group Video. MTV played it into heavy rotation despite the irony that its characters were made of televisions and slagging off television itself.

One word in the second verse has been edited, muted, or dropped for decades — Knopfler himself sang 'queenie' instead on a 1985 TV show, and sanitized radio edits have existed since the '90s. In 2011 Canada's broadcast council banned the unedited cut from radio, then reversed itself months later after fan outcry.
It remains Dire Straits' only US No. 1 — three weeks atop the Billboard Hot 100 — and it took home the 1986 Grammy for Best Rock Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal.
On August 1, 1987, MTV Europe launched and the very first video it ever aired was 'Money for Nothing' — the fitting final word for a song that opens and closes by demanding, 'I want my MTV.'

title: Sledgehammer
description: Peter Gabriel's stop-motion masterpiece: a claymation-and-pixilation joy-ride that turned a 1960s soul obsession into 1986's most unrepeatable pop moment.

pops.text: The video was commissioned by Tessa Watts at Virgin Records and directed by Stephen R. Johnson, who had just made Talking Heads' equally wild stop-motion clip for 'Road to Nowhere.' Gabriel picked him precisely because that earlier video had already blown his mind.

This was Gabriel's deliberate leap toward the pop mainstream: a love letter to the 1960s soul that made him want to be a musician. As a 17-year-old, he'd watched Otis Redding play London's Ram Jam club in 1967 and decided on the spot to go pro.

The horns are the real deal: a section led by Wayne Jackson of the Memphis Horns, the house band at Stax Records. Gabriel was thrilled — Jackson had toured with Otis Redding, the very singer he'd idolized as a teenager.

That eerie flute warbling through the song isn't a flute at all. Gabriel played a synthesized shakuhachi — a Japanese bamboo flute sound — using an E-mu Emulator II sampler, one of the era's hottest digital machines.

For one sequence, Gabriel lay motionless under a sheet of glass for 16 hours while animators painted clouds across his face frame by frame. Ten seconds of finished footage, painted on live. He later joked that if anyone wanted to copy the video, good luck to them.

Those dancing chickens bouncing to the shakuhachi solo were real, headless, featherless carcasses. The sequence was animated by a young Nick Park, who was still perfecting his plasticine technique — he'd later create Wallace & Gromit, and the birds reportedly started to stink as they rotted mid-shoot.

The whole production took 100 hours of shooting, with every second of finished video built from 25 unique poses of Gabriel. It was a true group effort: Aardman Animations and the experimental Brothers Quay tag-teamed the claymation, pixilation, and stop motion.

The song hit No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 on July 26, 1986 — knocking off his own former band. 'Sledgehammer' replaced Genesis's 'Invisible Touch' at the top, which remains the only American No. 1 for both Gabriel and Genesis. Phil Collins later joked they would've sent a telegram reading 'Congratulations — bastard.'

The video won nine MTV Video Music Awards in 1987 — still the most ever captured by a single video in one night — and Time later called it the most-played video in MTV history. Nearly forty years on, it remains the gold standard every music video is measured against.

title: In the Air Tonight
description: Phil Collins's brooding divorce-era slow burn that withholds its drums for three minutes — then detonates one of the most air-drummed fills in rock history.

pops.text: The song was written and recorded in the wreckage of Collins's divorce from his first wife — Face Value was essentially his emotional diary, and he's admitted he still isn't sure exactly what the lyrics are about.
Director Stuart Orme's video opens by literally animating the Face Value album cover: Collins's portrait fades in through the intro until his face fills the entire screen.
It started as a home demo built on a Roland CR-78 drum machine running its 'Disco-2' pattern, with ominous chords from a Prophet-5 synth — no real drums anywhere in the first minutes.

That colossal drum sound was an accident on someone else's record: while Collins played on Peter Gabriel's 'Intruder,' engineer Hugh Padgham had the studio's reverse-talkback mic channel open, and the brand-new SSL console's compressors and gates turned a casual drum take into a cannon blast that vanished in milliseconds. Padgham was brought into Face Value to recreate the trick — and gated reverb became the defining drum sound of the entire decade.

Released in January 1981, it shot to No. 2 in the UK — held off the top spot by John Lennon's posthumous 'Woman' — hit No. 1 in Germany, Sweden, Switzerland and Austria, and peaked at No. 19 on the US Billboard Hot 100 before going gold.

The famous urban legend — that Collins watched a man drown, saw another bystander refuse to help, and later sang the crime at him from the stage — is completely false. He has spent decades denying it; the words were improvised divorce-era feelings, not a confession.

The legendary drum fill lands around the 3:40 mark — fans call it the 'magic break' — and Collins later shrugged that it could have been anything; he just picked the spot where the drums should enter and played it in one go.

In 1984 the song's spooky groove backed the Miami Vice pilot, with Crockett and Tubbs cruising Miami at night in the Ferrari — so indelible a pairing that Collins later guested on the show as a con man in the episode 'Phil the Shill.'
In 2009, Mike Tyson's cameo in The Hangover made the fill comedy gold: Iron Mike air-drums it with total commitment, then plays the song on the piano.

In 2007, Cadbury's drumming-gorilla ad sent the song back onto the UK charts and to No. 1 in New Zealand for two weeks — his first chart-topper there — and the ad was later voted Britain's best-loved commercial of all time. The track has since landed at No. 35 on VH1's 100 Greatest Songs of the 80s and No. 291 on Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time.

title: I Wanna Dance with Somebody
description: The loudest, happiest, most neon breakup-proof anthem of the 80s — a three-and-a-half-minute serotonin bomb that has owned dance floors for four decades.

pops.text: The song was written by married couple George Merrill and Shannon Rubicam — the duo behind Whitney's earlier hit "How Will I Know," and the band Boy Meets Girl in their day job.

Director Brian Grant opens the video backstage in black and white, then explodes into a rainbow-colored dreamscape as Whitney ditches the conservative outfit for a crimped, Tina Turner-style blonde wig.
Merrill and Rubicam actually pitched a different song first: "Waiting for a Star to Fall." Clive Davis passed — and it went on to become a hit for Boy Meets Girl themselves.
When the demo was finally ready, Merrill sprinted through LAX to hand-deliver the cassette to Clive Davis before his plane took off.

Rubicam dreamed up the song during twilight walks on Venice Beach, picturing a single person dreading another lonely night — it was never about dancing, she said, but about wanting to do that dance of life with somebody.

Producer Narada Michael Walden first heard the demo and balked, saying it sounded like a rodeo tune suited to Olivia Newton-John. He slept on it, then rebuilt it with funkier Roland TR-808 drums and a synth-pop sheen.
The gamble paid off big: the single topped the charts in 17 countries and became Whitney's fourth straight No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100.
In 1988 it won the Grammy for Best Female Pop Vocal Performance — Whitney's second win in that category.
Talking Heads frontman David Byrne has covered the song on many occasions, once leading an entire stage of people in a group singalong at a 2017 Town Hall event celebrating his book How Music Works.

The song's legacy keeps growing: the 2022 Whitney Houston biopic took this song's title, and it's now a fixture at receptions everywhere — one outlet joked it's more relevant at weddings than "Here Comes the Bride."

title: Don't You (Forget About Me)
description: The Breakfast Club anthem Simple Minds never wanted to record — and it became the biggest, most defining hit of their career.

pops.text: The song was written specifically for The Breakfast Club by producer Keith Forsey — already an Oscar winner for the Flashdance theme — and guitarist Steve Schiff of the Nina Hagen band. They shaped it around a quiet scene where a shy kid and a school bully bond with no one watching.
Simple Minds turned it down more than once. They recorded only their own material, and guitarist Charlie Burchill later admitted they were laboring under delusions of being ultra-hip.

Before the band gave in, Bryan Ferry passed on it as badly timed while finishing his Boys and Girls album, and Billy Idol said no too — as did Cy Curnin of the Fixx. The label even floated Corey Hart, but Forsey vetoed the idea.

What finally tipped the scales: frontman Jim Kerr's then-wife Chrissie Hynde loved the song and badgered him to record it, and a few days hanging out with Forsey — whose work with Giorgio Moroder they admired — won the band over.

One account says the band rearranged and recorded the whole thing in about three hours in a north London studio in November 1984 — then promptly forgot about it, writing it off as a throwaway for a movie nobody would remember.

Released in February 1985, it hit No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 on May 18, knocking off Madonna's Crazy for You. It spent 22 weeks on the chart and remains Simple Minds' first and only American chart-topper, plus No. 1 in Canada and No. 7 in the UK.

The video was an early directing credit for Daniel Kleinman, shot inside Knebworth House in Hertfordshire. Kerr performs in a dark, chandelier-lit room crowded with rocking horses while clips from the film flicker on a wall of televisions.
The song's famous closing run of la-la-las wasn't written at all — Kerr improvised it on the spot in the studio. It became one of the most instantly recognizable codas in pop music.

On July 13, 1985, they played it at Live Aid in front of the JFK Stadium crowd in Philadelphia as part of a broadcast seen in 150 nations. Bob Geldof had insisted the newly famous-in-America Scots play the US show instead of Wembley.

The band left it off their next album, Once Upon a Time, uneasy about being defined by a song they didn't write — yet it became the one song every casual listener can name. Billy Idol finally recorded it for his 2001 Greatest Hits, and it still closes The Breakfast Club as Judd Nelson's reportedly improvised fist-pump freezes on screen.
